catalog_quote: Sapir’s transcription shows that accent placement in Nuuchahnulth is governed by a rather different rule from that found in Makah, formulated by Jacobsen (1979b: 4) as follows: “If the first vowel of a word is long, the accent falls on this syllable; if it is short, the accent falls on the second syllable.”[n.10] ... The Makah and Nuuchahnulth rules place accent identically except when the first two syllables are both short. In this case, Makah has accent on the second syllable, whereas Nuuchahnulth has accent on the first. ... [endnote 10, p. 350:] This rule correctly places primary accent in Makah, but there may be secondary accent at work as well since there are sometimes perceived prominences in addition to the primary accent, especially on long vowels. It is unclear whether these are merely phonetic correlates of vowel length or part of the accent system. Accent in Makah is stress …

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Both deciding quotations are verbatim at the stated locators in the Davidson 2002 text we hold (pp. 24-25, n.10 p. 350 = PDF 366) and Werle 2010 p. 16. (2) The classification (weight-sensitive, left edge, heavy = CVV only, primary on syllable 1 if long-vowelled else syllable 2) rests on a 2002 fieldwork dissertation endorsing the 1979 pedagogical sketch by the language's principal describer; Glottolog lists no fuller grammar or phonology of Makah, so nothing better exists to displace it. (3) Three additional open sources downloaded now from Werle's archive -- Werle 2002 (dedicated metrical analysis with his own Makah field data), Wilson 1986 (BLS 12:289) and Werle 2003 (instrumental vowel-length study) -- state or presuppose exactly the coded rule, including 'only syllables containing long vowels are heavy' and the two-syllable window; none contradicts. The only refinement is Werle 2010:16

sources.citation: Werle, Adam. 2002. The Southern Wakashan one-foot word. In C. Gillon, N. Sawai & R. Wojdak (eds.), Papers for the 37th International Conference on Salish and Neighbouring Languages (UBCWPL 9), 382-397. Vancouver: UBCWPL.
sources.quote: 'Stress in Makah is restricted to the first two syllables of the word, and appears to be predictable. ... (1) a. Makah: stress the first syllable if it is heavy, otherwise stress the second syllable. Only syllables containing long vowels are heavy. (Jacobsen 1979b, Davidson 2002)' with LĹ, LH́, H́L, H́H examples from Werle's own field notes; analysed as a single word-initial iamb (Hayes 1995); 'the stress never occurs later than the second syllable' even when a later heavy syllable follows light ones.
sources.note: Only dedicated metrical analysis of Makah stress with independent field data (consultants R. Claplanhoo, H. Swan); confirms H́X / LX́ with heavy = long vowel only and the two-syllable window; should be added to the record's sources.

sources.citation: Wilson, Stephen A. 1986. Metrical structure in Wakashan phonology. Proceedings of the 12th Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society, 283-291.
sources.quote: 'In Makah, stress falls on the first syllable if it is heavy, and on the second syllable if the first is light. This rule differs from Nootka only in the case where both syllables are light. Nootka would stress the first syllable, while Makah stresses the second.'
sources.locator: p. 7 (printed p. 289); image-only PDF, read via tesseract scanned
sources.note: Independent pre-Davidson statement of the same Makah rule (p. 289) in metrical terms; third confirmation.

sources.citation: Werle, Adam. 2003. The phonetic correlates of vowel length in Makah. Papers for ICSNL 38 (Lillooet, BC, 13-15 August 2003). University of Massachusetts, Amherst handout/paper, 8 pp.
sources.quote: Instrumental (Praat, 201 tokens, duration/F1/F2) study of the long/short vowel contrast, not of stress; test words were built 'Two syllables long, with a short vowel in the first syllable and the target vowel in a stressed second syllable' -- i.e. the design presupposes the coded rule (short V1 -> stress on syllable 2) but states no stress rule of its own.
sources.note: Only instrumental phonetic study of Makah found; bears on the CVV heavy class (length is cued by duration) but does not test stress placement.
